# Why cuBLAS GEMM scaling matters for attention
Self-attention in modern LLMs is dominated by matrix multiplications, but the way those GEMMs are implemented decides how and when the bottleneck of performance shifts.
In our technical deep dive, we analyzed the scaling performance of cuBLAS GEMMs. This post is a short companion to the full write-up. It summarizes what we measured, why it matters for real LLM workloads, and what you should expect before diving into the deeper profiling sections.

# What we tested
We benchmark four cuBLAS execution strategies on a single NVIDIA A100: (1) a “BigGemm” upper-bound baseline (collapse work into one large GEMM), (2) Iterative-GEMM (launch k independent GEMMs in a loop), (3) Batched-GEMM.
We sweep matrix size N across cache regimes (leveraging the A100’s 40 MB L2) and sweep batch size k until memory limits.

Then we repeat the scaling analysis using realistic attention GEMM shapes derived from Llama 3.1 (8B, 70B, 405B) for both training/prefill and inference decode.

# What you should expect from the detailed blog
1. Kernel launch overhead can dominate wall-clock time<br>
When GEMMs are small (e.g., cache-resident N), Iterative-GEMM scales poorly in wall-clock time because it pays per-head launch and synchronization costs. Batched execution largely amortizes that overhead, yielding huge end-to-end speedups at large k.

2. Batched is not always faster on GPU time<br>
On-device time behaves differently by regime. For small N, batching improves utilization and produces clear GPU-time speedups. For larger N (streaming regimes), batched kernels can be 20–30% slower than running single GEMMs, even though they still win strongly in wall-clock time.

3. The cache regime changes the “right” strategy<br>
As the working set crosses the L2 capacity, cuBLAS tiling/reuse behavior changes. The same algorithmic choice can move between compute-limited, latency-limited, and bandwidth-limited regimes depending on N and layout.

4. In Llama 3.1 training/prefill, time grows sharply with context length<br>
Mapping N to context length T and k to heads H, GPU time grows superlinearly with T (as expected from the T×T attention components), and the batched path tends to track the expected scaling more closely. Wall-clock time may stay flat at small T (overhead-dominated) and then “turn on” once kernel time dominates, especially for large models.

5. In decode inference, scaling looks different<br>
Decode introduces GEMV-like shapes (effectively M=1) and tends to show closer-to-linear growth with T for the batched path, while iterative can look artificially sub-linear at small shapes due to underutilization.

# Key takeaways
If you care about end-to-end latency, batching over heads is often the single biggest win because it amortizes kernel-launch overhead.
* GPU-time optimality is shape-dependent: batched GEMM can be slower than single GEMM for large matrices even while it wins in wall-clock time.
* Cache capacity (A100 40 MB L2) creates regime boundaries that materially change tiling, reuse, and achieved bandwidth.
* Real LLM shapes (Llama 3.1 8B/70B/405B) expose these effects clearly across both training/prefill and decode inference.
* HBM Pressure: High parallelism drives memory saturation. Batching hits a 75% bandwidth floor immediately, while iterative versions leave the GPU’s data pipe underutilized.
